newsitem.title: FINLAND: Low-key security for summit in freezing Finland.
newsitem.headline: Low-key security for summit in freezing Finland.

text.p: A well-oiled but low-key security operation swung into action in Finland on Wednesday as the freezing capital awaited the arrival of U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin.

The people of Helsinki, site of many superpower meetings in the past, barely shrugged as key locations were sealed off and menacing looking American and Russian secret service agents checked possible threats to their leaders.

At the grey-stoned Intercontinental Hotel, where Clinton will stay during the summit, the only noticeable change was the sudden blooming of thousands of daffodils, a bizarre phenomenon in sub-zero Helsinki where a light snow was falling.
On closer inspection, however, the flowers turned out to be artificial, planted in the barren soil to brighten the president's arrival.

"Winter is not over yet in Finland but we would like to brighten the place up," said a policeman outside the hotel, shivering in the icy wind slicing through the city, where an early spring ended abruptly earlier this week.
At Helsinki's Vantaa airport, where the two leaders will arrive, security officials were relaxed about the summit.
"I have been doing this job for 15 years and seen lots of meetings like this, it is no different," said Chief Superintendent Kauko Karhuvitta, in charge of security for the summit.
Karhuvitta said plane traffic would be disrupted slightly when Clinton and Yeltsin arrive in Helsinki around midday on Thursday, but that no major disruption was expected.
Clinton arrives on his Air Force One jumbo jet while Yeltsin is due to fly in aboard a new Ilyushin 96 jet.

Karhuvitta said there had been no threats to the two leaders and he did not expect any demonstrations to disrupt the meetings between the two leaders at Mantyniemi, the Finnish president's official residence.
"There is no need for threats. This is a summit for peace," he said.
At the Helsinki rescue centre, where emergency operations are coordinated, officials declined to give details of what plans had been laid to deal with terrorist actions or demonstrations.

Crime levels are traditionally low in Finland. The main civil disorder recently has come from motor bike gangs attacking each other. Alcohol, imbibed to lighten Finns' famous melancholic souls, is one of the leading causes of violence.
